cultivar: Kaihua local landrace and Fuding Dabai
processing: Baked green: single buds or bud-and-one-leaf shoots are fired, lightly rolled and straightened, then dried in two stages with warm air so the needle stays straight, downy and bright.
harvest_season: Spring, from late March to mid April; pre-Qingming bud lots are the showpiece grade.
appearance_dry: Straight, slender needles of silvery-green buds, heavily downy and very even.
appearance_liquor: Pale green-gold, clear with a faint haze of down.
appearance_wet: Plump buds and tiny leaves, bright green, standing upright then sinking.
taste_profile: Clean and sweet with orchid and fresh chestnut, a light umami body and a cool, refreshing finish.

brewing.notes: Tall glass, 80 °C. A bud tea for watching: the needles stand up, then fall. Keep the dose light.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, with pre-Qingming single-bud lots as the top grade and yu qian bud-and-leaf lots as the everyday version; mostly sold within Zhejiang. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Kaihua Long Ding is a bud tea from Kaihua county in western Zhejiang, where the province meets Anhui and Jiangxi near the source of the Qiantang river. The county's tea has old tribute records, and it has become one of Zhejiang's best-known greens.

It is baked rather than pan-dried, which matters: after firing, the slender shoots are straightened, not pressed, and dried with warm air, so the finished tea is a straight, downy needle that keeps its silvery colour and a fresh rather than roasty aroma. Good lots are striking in the tin, like a bundle of tiny silver-green spears.

The cup is clean and sweet, with orchid and fresh chestnut, a light savoury body and a cooling finish that lingers. It is gentle and three steeps is its range. Brew it in a tall glass at 80 °C, watch the needles stand and sink, and resist the urge to add more leaf; this is a tea of fragrance and texture, not strength.

It is sold as the current spring's harvest, graded by picking date and bud ratio, and most of it never leaves the province, so it is a good one to look for in Hangzhou or from a Zhejiang specialist. Pre-Qingming single-bud lots are the showpiece and priced that way; the bud-and-one-leaf tea picked a week or two later is better value and a touch fuller.

Tianmu Qing Ding from the mountains near Hangzhou is its nearest relative in style; try them together to see how two Zhejiang bud teas differ.
history:
Kaihua in western Zhejiang has an older tea record than its modern fame suggests: a local report traces written mentions to the late Tang, and it cites the county gazetteer for a tribute listing in 1631. How directly those teas connect to today's straight bud tea is unclear.

The name is tied by legend to Dalong Mountain in the county, whose summit tea was said to be especially good. The frying technique joined Zhejiang's provincial heritage list in 2009, and the name holds a geographical indication.
